defaults.permitted_development: Across Northamptonshire, the ordinary householder route for a fence, wall or gate usually depends on the height and its relationship to the road: 1 metre by a vehicular highway, 2 metres elsewhere. Listed-building settings and removed rights can change that answer quickly. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: Across Northamptonshire, for ordinary houses, most fence and wall questions come back to the same split between the 1 metre highway-side limit and the 2 metre limit elsewhere.
rules.depth_rules: Across Northamptonshire, a wall or fence is not assessed like an extension. The key issues are usually where it sits and how high it is, rather than how thick it is.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Northamptonshire, front and corner boundaries usually face the tightest control. Rear boundaries are generally less constrained than road-facing ones.
rules.roof_rules: Across Northamptonshire, canopies or roofed gate features need their own planning check.
rules.materials_rules: Across Northamptonshire, there is no prescribed material palette for ordinary fences and walls, but prominent frontages are easiest to justify when the boundary treatment fits the surrounding street character.

restrictions.conservation_area: A fence or wall in a conservation area may need more than a simple height check, especially if demolition of an older boundary is part of the scheme.
restrictions.listed_building: Boundary works to or around a listed building can require listed building consent, especially where historic walls, railings, piers or gates are being altered or removed.
restrictions.article4_notes: Normal enclosure rights can be withdrawn by Article 4 directions or by conditions on the property, which is why front-boundary work sometimes still needs an application.

rules.permitted_development: Boundary walls, fences and gates are usually permitted development if they stay no higher than 1 metre next to a highway used by vehicles and no higher than 2 metres elsewhere, or if an already-higher boundary is altered without increasing its height. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: A boundary treatment above the relevant height limit will normally need planning permission.
rules.depth_rules: A wall or fence is not assessed like an extension. The key issues are usually where it sits and how high it is, rather than how thick it is.
rules.boundary_rules: Front and corner boundaries usually face the tightest control. Rear boundaries are generally less constrained than road-facing ones.
rules.roof_rules: A simple gate or wall is one thing; a roofed gate feature can be quite another. Covered entrance elements should not be assumed to sit within the same fallback.
rules.materials_rules: National planning rules focus on height and siting rather than a fixed material list, but visible front boundaries should still use finishes that suit the house and street. Heritage areas are more demanding on detail.

restrictions.conservation_area: A fence or wall in a conservation area may need more than a simple height check, especially if demolition of an older boundary is part of the scheme.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building controls can apply to fences, gates and walls where they form part of the building's curtilage or historic setting.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions and site-specific conditions are a common reason why an otherwise modest boundary change still needs planning permission.
